scope: One consecutive record; full stored text, registered 1280x720 native/mobile image, independent reproduction of every $100K-to-$1M timeline, fee, inflation and crossover arithmetic, plus SPIVA, Marketing Science cash-out, Vanguard outlook and Fidelity 401(k)-millionaire checks

title.analysis: 'If You Have $100,000 Invested, Do THIS to Reach $1 Million' is a conditional self-qualifier ('If You Have $100,000 Invested') plus a withheld-action curiosity gap ('Do THIS') and a concrete round-number destination ('$1 Million'). The qualifier lets the viewer self-locate against a specific balance, which is the channel's most reliable framing, and the $100K-to-$1M promise is a recurring channel franchise. Same-channel comparisons on the same threshold vary widely: hvcr7gVbcr0 '$100,000 Means You're 1/3 Of The Way To $1,000,000 (The Surprising Math)' 2.85698x STRONG, GPSvnUVSl44 'Do This Once You Have $100,000 Saved' 2.51308x STRONG (nearly the same 'Do this' structure), 6RneApxqH1U '7 Things You Should Do Once You Have $100K Saved' 2.68484x STRONG and the age peer KrvtiC-Jaz0 'Let's Watch What Happens to People AFTER They Hit $100,000' 4.39531x STRONG; versus counterexamples MBtwn6xwamg 'Why $250K is Halfway to $1 Million (The Actual Math)' 1.00091x TYPICAL, QtXhRiEJ9zo 'Once You Hit $100K The Math Does The Rest' 0.81903x TYPICAL, ohQxPH0-adw 'Path From $100K To $1 Million (The Math They Don't Teach You)' 0.74675x TYPICAL and zppYzhlGiOc 'What $100K Invested Really Pays in Dividends (Realistically)' 0.46591x WEAK. This video (1.28087x TYPICAL) sits in the middle. Descriptively, the 'do this' and observational ('let's watch') variants appear in the STRONG group and 'path/math' explainers more often in TYPICAL or WEAK, but the sample is eight titles across different dates and channel sizes, and the $100K-to-$1M angle has been reused many times, so novelty fatigue is a plausible confounder. Not causal.
title.search_demand: Moderate explicit intent ('how long to turn 100k into 1 million', '100k to 1 million') exists as a calculator-style query, but the 'Do THIS' wording targets browse/suggested viewers already following the channel's $100K franchise. Historical query volume and traffic sources unavailable.
title.script_alignment: Partially aligned. The script does answer 'how long' with explicit timelines (33, 21 and just under 16 years) and closes with a six-item action list, but it explicitly admits the title's promise is not met in the expected way: 'I know it isn't what a video with this title is supposed to hand you. There's no secret allocation. There's nothing to buy.' The 'THIS' is effectively 'don't interrupt compounding': take the match, never cash out, cut fees, automate, own the market, raise the target. That is a defensible payoff but a deflation of the curiosity gap; viewers expecting a single tactic receive behavioural guardrails. It also partly contradicts the thumbnail's 'IT'S TOO EASY', since the script spends most of its runtime on why it feels slow and hard.

thumbnail.analysis: Registered maxresdefault fetched fresh and inspected at native 1280x720 and proportional 320x180. Pure white background. Left third: a cartoon man (ginger hair, large egg-shaped head, round eyes glancing sideways to the right, small pursed mouth, a skeptical or smug expression, grey T-shirt, blue jeans) holds a large light-blue cheque reading '$100K INVESTED' in bold black type, with small 'DATE 5/20/2024', 'PAY TO THE ORDER OF', 'DOLLARS' and a scribbled signature; his right index finger points right. Upper right: very large black condensed uppercase text 'IT'S TOO' on line one and 'EASY...' on line two, with an ellipsis. Lower centre: four green bar-chart columns rising left to right, with a thick black curved arrow sweeping from lower left over the bars toward a tan money sack labelled '$1 MILLION', surrounded by stacks of green banknotes. Reading path: headline text, then cheque, arrow, then money bag; the image tells a complete left-to-right story ($100K to growth to $1M). At 320px 'IT'S TOO EASY...' remains clearly legible, '$100K' and '$1 MILLION' are still readable though small, while 'INVESTED' and the cheque details become hard to read; black-on-white contrast holds and the green bars and money stacks stay distinct. Relationship: the thumbnail duplicates the title's $100K and $1 Million anchors and adds a new claim, 'IT'S TOO EASY...', which works as a contrarian curiosity hook but conflicts with the script, whose core message is that the path feels flat, slow and is usually abandoned (year-11 'Wednesday' scene, four things that 'take you out'). The ellipsis could be read as ironic, which would be consistent with the script, but that reading is not established. The cheque date 5/20/2024 is unexplained in the script. The cartoon-man style matches the generic illustrated style seen on other reviewed channel thumbnails; whether it is a recurring character was not verified. Historical continuity, A/B testing and CTR contribution are unverified.

script.opening_words: Your balance moved $400 this month. 400. You've got $100,000 sitting in there. You did everything right.
script.ending_words: So the question was never whether your money gets to a million. At 6 or 7% with anything automatic going in, it mathematically will. The question is whether you'll still be holding it when it does.
script.analysis: Full 17,198 canonical characters read in two contiguous chunks (0-10,000, 10,000-17,198). The hook is unusually concrete and second-person: a $400 monthly move on a $100,000 balance and the 'open the calculator ... close the tab and go make dinner' moment, which names a specific emotional state the target viewer has likely had. It then opens a strong loop with two women, same fund and return, $410,000 versus $940,000, and 'which one are you currently on track to be?'. The weakness is that this loop is never explicitly closed: the women do not return, and the arithmetic implies the gap is mostly contribution size (about $395 versus $2,067 a month at 7%), not the 'four things' the video goes on to list. The three-part roadmap is stated early and kept, which gives clean structure. Part one's 'crossover line' is the most original idea in the script: a calculable milestone (about $86,000 at $500 a month) that reframes the viewer as already past something, delivered with a dry joke ('Congratulations. Nobody sent a card'). Part two uses a named character (Ranata) and asks the viewer to 'find yourself' in three timelines, then pivots with a crisp claim ('You think the lever you're pulling is money. It's not. It's time'). The first-five versus last-five comparison is rhetorically effective (the 'used Camry spread across an entire presidential term' line) but numerically switches to a zero-contribution, 30-year path that contradicts Ranata's stated $1,000-a-month, 21-year plan. The year-11 'ordinary Wednesday' scene is the best-written beat: it names the specific moment of quitting, lists concrete temptations (Bitcoin screenshot, rental property at a red light) and reframes flatness as the shape of an exponential curve, with the 'half the theater walks out in the second act' metaphor. Part three's transitions are explicitly rank-ordered ('Number two is the one that actually does the damage', 'the one nobody warns you about'), and each risk gets a character or a number, which keeps the list from feeling generic; the Nadia kitchen-counter scene with the movers waiting is especially vivid and is used to explain choice architecture rather than blame the viewer. A notable credibility technique is the self-steelman ('let me argue against myself') and then turning skepticism on his own side (Dalbar versus Morningstar versus the Financial Analysts Journal paper), which signals honesty. The payoff list is short and actionable, and the script candidly admits the title promises a secret it will not deliver. The ending resolves all three characters (but not the two women from the hook) and closes on a memorable line ('not interrupt it while it finishes'). Weaknesses: the return-assumption section mixes a '6% real' return with an inflation-adjusted $1.6 million target, double counting inflation; Desmond's 'adds four years' does not reproduce under the video's own assumptions; several statistics are attributed to named firms without enough detail to check; the Fidelity count appears higher than the latest published figure; and there are two subscribe asks plus two community plugs. All stored text read; not an original-audio, editing or retention verification.

claim_audit: Timelines reproduced independently (analyst Python; assumptions: $100,000 start, end-of-month contributions, nominal annual rate compounded monthly, no fees, no taxes, no inflation adjustment; annual-compounding variants in parentheses). Narrator 'put in nothing at all ... a million in about 33 years' at 7%: 32.99 years monthly (34.03 annual) - CORRECT. '$1,000 a month ... there in 21': 20.95 years (21.61 annual) - CORRECT. '2,000 a month, just under 16': 15.89 years (16.40 annual) - CORRECT only under monthly compounding. 'Doubling your contribution ... buys you 5 years': 20.95 - 15.89 = 5.06 years - CORRECT. '$500 a month' (implied): 25.30 years.

'At 6%, Ranata's $1,000 a month takes 23 years instead of 21': 23.16 years at 6% monthly (23.79 annual) - arithmetic CORRECT. Conceptual error: the narrator says 'build your plan at 6% real' and in the same section raises the target to $1.6 million to offset inflation. Using a real return and an inflation-inflated nominal target double counts inflation; a 6% real plan should target about $1 million in today's dollars, or a nominal plan should use about 8.5% nominal (6% real plus 2.5% inflation). Also, the Vanguard figures he cites (about 4 to 6%) are nominal 10-year forecasts, so 6% real is above the forecast he invokes, not below it.

Crossover line: '$100,000 throws off about $7,000 a year' at 7% - CORRECT. '$500 a month ... crossed it somewhere around $86,000': 6,000 / 0.07 = $85,714 - CORRECT. '$1,000 a month, you cross at about 171,000': 12,000 / 0.07 = $171,429 - CORRECT. Note that 7% is an expected average, not a guaranteed annual 'throw-off'; in a down year the market contributes negative dollars.
'3.32 doublings' for 10x: log2(10) = 3.3219 - CORRECT. 'At 7% your money doubles about every 10 years': 10.24 years - CORRECT.

First five versus last five years: 'She goes from 100,000 to about 140 grand over five years' matches only the zero-contribution path (100,000 x 1.07^5 = $140,255 annual; $141,763 monthly). With Ranata's stated $1,000 a month, the year-5 balance is about $213,355 (analyst calculation). '760,000 to over a million' also matches the zero-contribution annual path (100,000 x 1.07^30 = $761,226; x 1.07^35 = $1,067,658, gain $306,432) and 'she'd already been doing it for 30 years', but Ranata was introduced as reaching $1 million in 21 years with $1,000 a month. The illustration silently switches to a different scenario. The stored text reads '$36,000 in five years'; given 'seven and a half times the money' (about $306,000 / $40,000 = 7.6), this is likely an ASR error for '$306,000' - flagged UNCERTAIN, not corrected against audio.

'Ranata ... 11 years in. The balance says about $400,000 ... she isn't even halfway ... she's 49': $1,000 a month path gives $413,484 at year 11 (analyst calculation); 38 + 11 = 49; under halfway to $1 million - CORRECT within rounding.

'What does waiting 3 years to get serious cost you? 3 years': true only if the whole $100,000 also sits idle. If the $100,000 keeps compounding and only the $1,000 contributions are delayed three years, the total time becomes about 22.77 years, a delay cost of about 1.82 years, not 3 (analyst calculation). Ambiguous wording; partially overstated.

Two-women cold open ('$410,000' versus '$940,000' after 15 years, same fund, same return): no contribution figures are ever stated, so not reproducible from the script. At 7% monthly, the gap would require about $395 a month versus about $2,067 a month of contributions (analyst back-solve) - i.e. the difference is mostly savings rate, not the 'four things'. The open loop 'where did half a million dollars go?' is never explicitly answered; the women do not return.

Fees: '$100,000, 30 years, 7%, 0.03% fee about $755,000; 1% fee about $574,000; $180,000 gone': 100,000 x 1.0697^30 = $754,849 and 100,000 x 1.06^30 = $574,349, gap $180,500 (analyst calculation, fee subtracted from return annually) - CORRECT. Later 'If it starts with a one, you're looking at a $200,000 problem' rounds this upward.

Desmond: '$100,000 ... gets there in 20 years' then 'resets to 1.6 million, adds four years'. Contributions are not stated. With constant contributions sized to hit $1 million in 20 years at 7% (about $1,144 a month), reaching $1.6 million takes 25.82 years, i.e. about 5.8 extra years; at 6% (about $1,448 a month) about 6.4 extra years. 'Four years' is reproduced only with zero contributions and about 12.2% annual return (10^(1/20) - 1), which conflicts with the video's own 6% advice. Flag: 'adds four years' is UNDERSTATED under the video's own assumptions (analyst calculation).

Inflation: 'At 2.5% inflation, a million 20 years from now buys what about 610,000 buys you today': 1,000,000 / 1.025^20 = $610,271 - CORRECT. 'Closer to 1.6 million': 1,000,000 x 1.025^20 = $1,638,616 - CORRECT. 'Sheds about half its meaning every 25 years': 1/1.025^25 = 0.539 - approximately correct at 2.5%. 'Your million dollars today buys what 375,000 bought in 1990': using CPI-U annual averages of about 130.7 (1990) and about 322 (2025, analyst-recalled, not re-fetched) gives about $406,000; $375,000 implies a price ratio of 2.67, somewhat higher than CPI-U indicates - UNVERIFIED, likely overstated.

Return assumptions: 'Vanguard's 10-year outlook for US stocks is roughly 4 to 6%': Vanguard's December 2025 outlook listed 4.0% to 5.0% for US equities and its January 2026 model run about 3.9% to 5.9% (nominal) - broadly CONSISTENT, available before publication. 'Goldman around 6 1/2' - not checked, UNVERIFIED. 'Build it at 10, get six, and you find out it's 63' is unclear in the stored text (possibly 'at 63' as an age); a $1,000-a-month plan built at 10% reaches $1 million in 16.34 years, but at 6% over the same period reaches only about $597,000 (analyst calculation). Possible ASR or phrasing issue flagged UNCERTAIN.

'Research published in Marketing Science tracking over 160,000 departing employees found it's 41.4% ... 85% of those people empty the account completely': Wang, Zhai and Lynch, 'Cashing Out Retirement Savings at Job Separation', Marketing Science 42(4) 2023: 162,360 terminating employees in 28 plans, 41.4% cashed out; about 64% emptied in one transaction plus 21% over multiple withdrawals (= 85%) - CONSISTENT (secondary press coverage and university listing; paper not opened). Calling 41.4% 'a coin flip' is rhetorical. '$266,000 lifetime cost' - source not named, UNVERIFIED.

'The most recent SPIVA scorecard found 79% of active large cap US funds underperformed the S&P 500 last year': SPIVA U.S. Year-End 2025 reports about 79% - CORRECT, available before publication. 'Over 15 years about 90%' and 'not a single one of 22 US equity categories' - not checked in this review, UNVERIFIED.

'Fidelity counts about $850,000 401k millionaires right now. Roughly 1 and a half% ... They averaged about 26 years': Fidelity's Q2 2026 data (secondary coverage, released before the 2026-08-23 publication) reported a record 769,000 401(k) millionaires with an average saving tenure of about 25 years. The '850,000' does not match the latest figure found - likely OVERSTATED or from an unidentified source; the 1.5% share was not checked. Note the stored text has '$850,000', a probable ASR artefact for '850,000' people (UNCERTAIN).

'Over the 20 years through 2025, staying fully invested roughly 7xed your money. Miss only the 10 best days, you end with about half'; 'Seven of those 10 best days landed within 2 weeks of one of the 10 worst days'; 'Morning Star found the median gap ... is seven days': no primary source found in this review - UNVERIFIED. A 7x multiple over 20 years implies about 10.2% a year (analyst calculation), plausible for S&P 500 total return but not confirmed. Vanguard 2020 'fewer than half of 1% went fully to cash', '$24 billion' forfeited match, Morningstar '1.2 percentage points' gap, target-date funds 'about a tenth of a percentage point', and the Financial Analysts Journal 'tenth of 1%' paper were not checked - UNVERIFIED.

'At 6 or 7% with anything automatic going in, it mathematically will' reach a million: true only as an eventual limit; with zero contributions 6% takes 38.47 years and with small contributions decades, and real (inflation-adjusted) $1 million is a different target, which the video itself just argued. It also presents expected returns as certain.

Possible ASR artefacts preserved, not corrected against audio: 'about$7,000', 'a,000 a month' / 'a th000' (likely '$1,000'), 'a h 100,000 to about 140 40 grand', 'Ranata' / 'ranada', '300ths of 1%' and '300s of a percent' (likely 'three hundredths'), 'Morning Star', 'Spya' (likely 'SPIVA'), 'Financial Analyst Journal', 'school community' (likely 'Skool'), '$850,000' for a count of people, and '$36,000' for a likely $306,000.

topic.analysis: Compounding timelines from $100,000 to $1 million, framed around behaviour rather than asset selection: crossover point, time versus contribution as levers, the psychological flat middle, and four failure modes (fees, 401(k) cash-out at job change, panic selling, inflation-eroded targets), followed by realistic return assumptions and a six-item checklist. Evergreen; intermediate audience with existing savings; strong household relevance. Distinctive audience question: 'I have $100K, why does it feel like nothing is happening and how long until $1M?' The behavioural and choice-architecture framing (Nadia's one-box cash-out) is more differentiated than a plain compound-interest table, but the $100K-to-$1M topic has been covered repeatedly on this channel.
topic.novelty_and_corpus_angle: Original opportunity: build a fully consistent version with one explicit assumption set (start balance, contribution, nominal or real return, fees, inflation) carried through every timeline, a closed cold-open loop (show exactly which contribution or failure mode produced the $410,000 versus $940,000 gap), and a clean real-versus-nominal treatment (either 6% real with a $1 million real target, or about 8.5% nominal with a $1.6 million nominal target). The crossover-line milestone and the 'ordinary Wednesday' quitting moment are the strongest reusable ideas; cite the Marketing Science cash-out study and SPIVA directly.

virality.analysis: Observed result: 6,067 frozen views at 18.0753 days; ten-peer ratio 1.28087x TYPICAL and five-peer ratio 1.41064x TYPICAL, both independently reproduced; the tier agrees across peer windows, so it is not peer-sensitive. Likes 215 (3.54% of views) and comments 54 (0.89%). The video is young (18 days) and its absolute views are low relative to older channel uploads, so the age-matched ratio, not raw views, is the relevant comparison. Evidence-backed interpretation: among its ten age peers, the three STRONG videos (KrvtiC-Jaz0 4.39531x, 4vUg_DFIwes 2.13326x, g2nNpY3rHaU 2.06834x) use an observational 'let's watch', a named system or a list of wasteful purchases, while the closest topical peers (MBtwn6xwamg '$250K is Halfway to $1 Million' 1.00091x, dJqAfhcX5lw '$1M, $2M, and $5M Retirement' 0.50009x) are TYPICAL, like this one. Hypotheses: (a) the $100K-to-$1M promise is a heavily reused channel franchise, which may limit novelty for returning viewers; (b) the 'Do THIS' curiosity gap is similar to GPSvnUVSl44 (2.51308x STRONG), so the title structure alone is unlikely to explain the TYPICAL result; (c) the thumbnail's 'IT'S TOO EASY...' contrarian claim may attract clicks but conflicts with the script's 'it feels slow' message; (d) comment rate of 0.89% is relatively high, consistent with the script's explicit 'tell me where you are on that timeline' prompt. Proposed experiment: in owned uploads, test the same script under a crossover-milestone title (for example 'You Already Passed the Hardest Point at $86K') versus a 'Do THIS to reach $1M' title, and an 'IT'S TOO EASY' versus 'WHY IT FEELS SLOW' thumbnail, measuring CTR, impressions and retention at the year-11 scene and the start of part three. None of these hypotheses is measurable here without impressions, CTR, traffic sources or retention.

original_content_lesson.test: Produce a $100K-to-$1M video with one consistent, stated assumption set, a closed cold-open loop, and a clean real-versus-nominal target; test crossover-milestone packaging against 'Do THIS' packaging, and 'feels slow' versus 'too easy' thumbnails, in owned experiments measuring CTR, retention at each part boundary and comment rate.
